"title": "Frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions in TbB4",
"authors": "T. Inami, K. Ohwada, Y. H. Matsuda, Z. W. Ouyang, H. Nojiri, D. Okuyama, T. Matsumura, and Y. Murakami",
"field_subfield": "Condensed matter physics; magnetism of frustrated rare-earth compounds",
"type_of_paper": "Research letter",
"executive_summary": "This letter reports resonant magnetic x-ray diffraction (RMXD) experiments on the Shastry-Sutherland-lattice compound TbB4, performed under strong pulsed magnetic fields up to 29 T. TbB4 is a rare-earth tetra-boride that crystallizes in the tetragonal space group P4/mbm and whose rare-earth network is equivalent to the geometrically frustrated Shastry-Sutherland lattice. The material has two magnetic transition temperatures, TN1 = 44 K and TN2 = 22 K, and below TN2 its magnetic moments are confined to the basal ab-plane with additional in-plane anisotropy orienting them along the diagonal. For an XY-type magnet, one would anticipate a linear magnetization process when the field is applied along the c-axis, yet TbB4 instead exhibits a multi-step metamagnetic behavior between 16 and 28 T, with a reported 9 steps and a prominent one-half magnetization plateau. The authors argue that this curve is difficult to predict because TbB4 has an XY-type ground state. The central experimental advance is the observation of the 100 magnetic reflection intensity as a function of field. The net diffraction intensity of the 100 reflection is about 2x10^5 counts/s, marginally strong enough for a pulsed-field experiment. Two key outcomes emerge: first, a considerable amount of the 100 reflection intensity remains in the magnetization plateau phases above 16 T, decreasing with increasing field above 16 T and staying constant between 20 and 24 T, where the one-half plateau is observed; second, the characteristic polarization dependence of RMXD shows that the observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of ab-plane components rather than the c-axis component. This is surprising because plateau phases are usually expected to have collinear structures with no ordered moment perpendicular to the field. From these data, the authors deduce a simple spin model in which the ground state is a very hard XY spin with in-plane anisotropy E and the excited state is an Ising spin with energy gap D, and they calculate the magnetization curve. The one-half plateau is clearly reproduced, and the diffracted intensity of the corresponding structure is about one-quarter of the ground state, broadly consistent with the observed intensity of about 30-50% of the intensity at 0 T. Similar results were obtained with other parameter sets and cell sizes (2x2 and 1x3 cells). The authors propose that frustration is the key to understanding the observed multi-step magnetization, because frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the successive metamagnetic transitions. The paper emphasizes the integration of RMXD using brilliant third-generation synchrotron radiation and excellent pulsed-magnetic-field techniques, which enables exploration of magnetic structures at high fields close to 30 T.",

summary.title: Frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions in TbB4
summary.authors: T. Inami, K. Ohwada, Y. H. Matsuda, Z. W. Ouyang, H. Nojiri, D. Okuyama, T. Matsumura, and Y. Murakami
summary.field_subfield: Condensed matter physics; magnetism of frustrated rare-earth compounds
summary.executive_summary: This letter reports resonant magnetic x-ray diffraction (RMXD) experiments on the Shastry-Sutherland-lattice compound TbB4, performed under strong pulsed magnetic fields up to 29 T. TbB4 is a rare-earth tetra-boride that crystallizes in the tetragonal space group P4/mbm and whose rare-earth network is equivalent to the geometrically frustrated Shastry-Sutherland lattice. The material has two magnetic transition temperatures, TN1 = 44 K and TN2 = 22 K, and below TN2 its magnetic moments are confined to the basal ab-plane with additional in-plane anisotropy orienting them along the diagonal. For an XY-type magnet, one would anticipate a linear magnetization process when the field is applied along the c-axis, yet TbB4 instead exhibits a multi-step metamagnetic behavior between 16 and 28 T, with a reported 9 steps and a prominent one-half magnetization plateau. The authors argue that this curve is difficult to predict because TbB4 has an XY-type ground state. The central experimental advance is the observation of the 100 magnetic reflection intensity as a function of field. The net diffraction intensity of the 100 reflection is about 2x10^5 counts/s, marginally strong enough for a pulsed-field experiment. Two key outcomes emerge: first, a considerable amount of the 100 reflection intensity remains in the magnetization plateau phases above 16 T, decreasing with increasing field above 16 T and staying constant between 20 and 24 T, where the one-half plateau is observed; second, the characteristic polarization dependence of RMXD shows that the observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of ab-plane components rather than the c-axis component. This is surprising because plateau phases are usually expected to have collinear structures with no ordered moment perpendicular to the field. From these data, the authors deduce a simple spin model in which the ground state is a very hard XY spin with in-plane anisotropy E and the excited state is an Ising spin with energy gap D, and they calculate the magnetization curve. The one-half plateau is clearly reproduced, and the diffracted intensity of the corresponding structure is about one-quarter of the ground state, broadly consistent with the observed intensity of about 30-50% of the intensity at 0 T. Similar results were obtained with other parameter sets and cell sizes (2x2 and 1x3 cells). The authors propose that frustration is the key to understanding the observed multi-step magnetization, because frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the successive metamagnetic transitions. The paper emphasizes the integration of RMXD using brilliant third-generation synchrotron radiation and excellent pulsed-magnetic-field techniques, which enables exploration of magnetic structures at high fields close to 30 T.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This letter reports resonant magnetic x-ray diffraction (RMXD) experiments on the Shastry-Sutherland-lattice compound TbB4, performed under strong pulsed magnetic fields up to 29 T. TbB4 is a rare-earth tetra-boride that crystallizes in the tetragonal space group P4/mbm and whose rare-earth network is equivalent to the geometrically frustrated Shastry-Sutherland lattice. The material has two magnetic transition temperatures, TN1 = 44 K and TN2 = 22 K, and below TN2 its magnetic moments are confined to the basal ab-plane with additional in-plane anisotropy orienting them along the diagonal. For an XY-type magnet, one would anticipate a linear magnetization process when the field is applied along the c-axis, yet TbB4 instead exhibits a multi-step metamagnetic behavior between 16 and 28 T, with a reported 9 steps and a prominent one-half magnetization plateau. The authors argue that this curve is difficult to predict because TbB4 has an XY-type ground state. The central experimental advance is the observation of the 100 magnetic reflection intensity as a function of field. The net diffraction intensity of the 100 reflection is about 2x10^5 counts/s, marginally strong enough for a pulsed-field experiment. Two key outcomes emerge: first, a considerable amount of the 100 reflection intensity remains in the magnetization plateau phases above 16 T, decreasing with increasing field above 16 T and staying constant between 20 and 24 T, where the one-half plateau is observed; second, the characteristic polarization dependence of RMXD shows that the observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of ab-plane components rather than the c-axis component. This is surprising because plateau phases are usually expected to have collinear structures with no ordered moment perpendicular to the field. From these data, the authors deduce a simple spin model in which the ground state is a very hard XY spin with in-plane anisotropy E and the excited state is an Ising spin with energy gap D, and they calculate the magnetization curve. The one-half plateau is clearly reproduced, and the diffracted intensity of the corresponding structure is about one-quarter of the ground state, broadly consistent with the observed intensity of about 30-50% of the intensity at 0 T. Similar results were obtained with other parameter sets and cell sizes (2x2 and 1x3 cells). The authors propose that frustration is the key to understanding the observed multi-step magnetization, because frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the successive metamagnetic transitions. The paper emphasizes the integration of RMXD using brilliant third-generation synchrotron radiation and excellent pulsed-magnetic-field techniques, which enables exploration of magnetic structures at high fields close to 30 T.

Research Context
Magnetization plateaus are a hallmark of several magnetic materials, arising from mechanisms such as zero compressibility and Sz being a good quantum number. Ising-type antiferromagnets with competing J1 and J2 interactions are the most comprehensible class, producing step-like magnetization curves. Examples of Ising-type plateaus include the one-third plateau of CoCl2·2H2O and the multi-step curves of PrCo2Si2 and CeSb. Magnetization plateaus also occur for Heisenberg spins, including isolated dimers and orthogonally connected dimer systems. Geometrically frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnets such as triangular- and pyrochlore-lattice systems exhibit one-third and one-half plateaus. A crucial point is that all plateau phases have a collinear magnetic structure with no ordered moment perpendicular to the field. TbB4 was recently found to exhibit a multi-step magnetization curve that resembles none of the previously known magnets. To the authors' best knowledge, CsFeCl3 is considered to be the only example of a magnet with ordered perpendicular components in the plateau phase. In these perpendicular-component magnets, frustration plays a central role in the multi-step magnetization process.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is why TbB4 exhibits a multi-step magnetization process that is hardly predicted for an XY-type ground state. The authors hypothesize that the plateau phases are accompanied by large XY components of magnetic moments, contrary to the usual collinear expectation. The authors predict that the observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of ab-plane components rather than the c-axis component. The authors hypothesize that a simple spin model with a very hard XY ground state and excited Ising spins can reproduce the magnetization curve. The authors predict that frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the observed multi-step metamagnetic behavior. The authors predict that the one-half plateau is clearly reproduced by the model, with a diffracted intensity of about one-quarter of the ground state. The authors predict that the critical field of the one-third plateau phase is inevitably smaller than that of the one-half plateau phase. The authors predict that the proposed model captures basic features of the real TbB4 despite being simplified.

Methodological Details
The study used single crystals of TbB4 grown by the floating zone method. The experiments were carried out at undulator beamline BL22XU at SPring-8. The x-ray energy was tuned to the Tb LIII absorption edge at 7.514 keV. Magnetic fields up to 29 T were generated using a small pulsed magnet with a 0.6 ms pulse duration. The magnet is a split-pair with two windows prepared for incoming and outgoing x-rays. The magnet and sample were attached to the cold head of a conventional closed cycle refrigerator. A high-counting-rate detector, an avalanche photodiode, was used with a typical resolution of 10 µs. The scattering plane was horizontal with the a* axis in the plane, and magnetic fields were vertical and parallel to the c-axis. The field strength was monitored as a function of time to obtain the field dependence of the diffraction intensity. The sample surface was locally heated by irradiation of synchrotron x-rays, and the true sample temperature was estimated by measuring the temperature dependence of the magnetic peak intensity. The data for the field dependence of the 100 reflection at 18 K were an average of 30 field-scans. The net diffraction intensity of the 100 reflection is about 2x10^5 counts/s, marginally strong enough for a pulsed-field experiment.

Procedures And Architectures
The spin Hamiltonian includes XY interactions, Ising interactions, in-plane anisotropy E, energy gap D, and the Zeeman term. The spins are treated as unit vectors in the Hamiltonian. Magnetization curves were calculated for finite-size cells with periodic boundary conditions. The authors consider 4 spins in the crystallographic unit cell (1x1 cell). For simplicity, the authors initially consider the limit E →∞, so each spin has only 4 states. The authors took J1 = 2, J2 = 1, J3 = 2, D = 1 for the calculations. The calculated magnetization curve is shown in Fig. 4(a), and the one-half magnetization plateau is clearly reproduced. Similar results were obtained with other sets of parameters and different cell sizes (2x2 and 1x3 cells). The authors set the in-plane anisotropy E finite to allow moments to rotate in the ab-plane, treating Ising sites as defects. The authors note that interactions further than J3 must be included to account for the splitting at Hc1.

Key Results
The 100 reflection intensity remains in the magnetization plateau phases above 16 T, decreasing with increasing field and staying constant between 20 and 24 T. The constant intensity between 20 and 24 T corresponds to the one-half magnetization plateau phase. The plateau phases include the (1,0,0) component in their magnetic structures. The observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of the ab-plane components rather than the c-axis component. The diffracted intensity of the one-half plateau structure is about one-quarter of the ground state. The diffracted intensity is broadly consistent with the observed intensity of about 30-50% of the intensity at 0 T. The one-half magnetization plateau is clearly reproduced by the model. The critical field of the one-third plateau phase is inevitably smaller than that of the one-half plateau phase. Many states are degenerate at the critical fields Hc1/2 and Hc1 when E=∞. The magnetic intensity observed in the plateau phases illustrates that large XY-components of the magnetic moments coexist with aligned Z-components. The magnetic moments in the one-third plateau phase are rearranged to reduce the total energy. The resultant magnetic lattice of the one-half plateau phase is not frustrated, as illustrated by collinear in-plane components.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The plateau phases have large XY components of magnetic moments, contrary to the usual collinear expectation. A canted magnetic structure would result in a continuous magnetization curve unlike the observed step-like process. The plateau phases consist of very hard XY-type magnetic moments and Ising-like magnetic moments. Frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the observed multi-step metamagnetic behavior. Frustration is not only an origin of degenerate states, but also breaks degeneracy. The basic scenario that frustration lifts the degeneracy at a metamagnetic transition is common for both TbB4 and CsFeCl3. Frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions are a general mechanism. The proposed spin model captures basic features of the real TbB4 despite being simplified.

Contradictions And Limitations
The proposed spin model is very much simplified, with no cross-term between the XY and Ising spins. The model is a simplification, but the authors believe it captures basic features of the real TbB4. The authors acknowledge that the spin models for TbB4 and CsFeCl3 are quite different. The degeneracy at the critical fields is a normal phenomenon, but if this degeneracy is lifted, the multi-step magnetization curve can be reproduced. The proposed model is a hypothesis that requires further validation. The one-half plateau is reproduced, but the one-third plateau is only proposed as a possible magnetic structure. The sample surface was locally heated by irradiation of synchrotron x-rays, which could affect the measurements. The net diffraction intensity of the 100 reflection is marginally strong enough for a pulsed-field experiment.

Claims
The plateau phases of TbB4 have large XY components of magnetic moments, contrary to the usual collinear expectation. The 100 reflection intensity remains in the plateau phases above 16 T. The observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of the ab-plane components. The magnetic intensity illustrates that large XY-components coexist with aligned Z-components. A canted magnetic structure would result in a continuous magnetization curve unlike the observed step-like process. It is expected that all magnetic moments in plateau phases are parallel or antiparallel to the field. The plateau phases consist of very hard XY-type magnetic moments and Ising-like magnetic moments. Frustration plays a central role in the multi-step magnetization process.
Frustration is the key to understanding the observed multi-step magnetization, lifting the degeneracy at the critical fields. The frustrated nature of the SS lattice lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields. The basic scenario that frustration lifts the degeneracy at a metamagnetic transition is common for both magnets. Frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions are a general mechanism. Classical continuous spins on the SS lattice are not frustrated in the strict sense. The degeneracy at the critical fields is a normal phenomenon observed in metamagnetic transitions. Frustration is not only an origin of degenerate states, but also breaks degeneracy. The proposed spin model captures basic features of the real TbB4.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Similar results were obtained with other sets of parameters and different cell sizes (2x2 and 1x3 cells). The one-half plateau is reproduced with the limit E →∞, and the model is simplified.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 shows examples of magnetization plateaus: ground states (left) and magnetization plateau phases (right). Fig. 2(a) shows the magnetic structure of TbB4 between TN1 and TN2, and Fig. 2(b) shows the magnetization process. Fig. 3(a) shows the incident energy dependence of the 100 reflection, Fig. 3(b) shows the temperature dependence, and Fig. 3(c) shows the field dependence. Fig. 4(a) shows the calculated magnetization curve for E →∞, Fig. 4(b) shows a possible magnetic structure of the one-third plateau phase, and Fig. 4(c) shows the schematic energy diagram.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that TbB4 has large XY components of magnetic moments in the plateau phases, revealing a new class of frustrated magnets. 2. The strongest evidence is the observation that the observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of the ab-plane components. 3. The future path is the application of RMXD and pulsed-magnetic-field techniques to explore magnetic structures at high fields close to 30 T.
